title: Understand star schema and the importance for Power BI
summary: Microsoft's practitioner guidance on star schema design specifically for Power BI semantic models, covering normalization vs. denormalization, measures, surrogate keys, snowflake dimensions, slowly changing dimensions (Type 1/Type 2), role-playing dimensions, junk dimensions, degenerate dimensions, and factless fact tables.
audience: Power BI Desktop data modelers building semantic models who need to translate classic dimensional-modeling theory into Power BI-specific relationship and DAX design decisions.
why_it_matters: It's the bridge document between generic Kimball-style dimensional modeling and the concrete constraints of Power BI's relationship engine — such as the single-active-relationship limitation — which materially changes how patterns like role-playing dimensions and Type 2 SCDs must be implemented in a semantic model versus a warehouse.
takeaways: Power BI's single-active-relationship-per-table-pair rule is the key constraint that shapes several modeling patterns, especially role-playing dimensions.
Power Query alone cannot construct a Type 2 slowly changing dimension from source data; that logic must live upstream in a data warehouse ETL process.
Table type (fact vs. dimension) in a Power BI model is determined by relationship cardinality, not by any explicit table property.
Several named patterns (junk dimensions, degenerate dimensions, factless fact tables) exist specifically to control model storage size and Data pane clutter.
Denormalizing snowflake dimensions into a single table is generally preferred in Power BI for storage and usability, with hierarchy support as a bonus.

claims.text: In a Power BI semantic model, whether a table behaves as a dimension or a fact table is determined entirely by relationship cardinality, not by any explicit table property; the 'one' side of a one-to-many relationship is always the dimension.
A well-structured Power BI model should not mix dimension and fact roles in a single table, and fact tables should always load data at a consistent grain.

Snowflake dimensions (normalized into multiple related tables, e.g. category/subcategory/product) can be denormalized into a single Power BI model table; Microsoft generally recommends this because it reduces model tables, shortens relationship filter-propagation chains, and enables cross-column hierarchies that a snowflake design cannot support.

A Power BI semantic model can only have one active relationship between any two tables; alternate relationships must be set inactive and can only be invoked in DAX via the USERELATIONSHIP function, which forces manual measure creation for each alternate role.

For role-playing dimensions (e.g. a date table used for order date, ship date, and delivery date), the recommended Power BI pattern is to create a separate dimension table per role using a referenced Power Query or DAX calculated table, each with its own single active relationship, rather than relying on inactive relationships and USERELATIONSHIP.

Power Query alone cannot implement a Type 2 slowly changing dimension (versioned dimension rows with start/end date validity); that change-detection logic must run upstream, typically in a data warehouse ETL/load process, and the semantic model then loads the pre-built SCD Type 2 table.
A Type 1 slowly changing dimension is achieved in Power BI simply by a non-incremental table refresh, which overwrites dimension rows with the latest source values and discards prior state.

A surrogate key is a unique identifier added to a dimension table (not present in source data) so it can serve as the 'one' side of a Power BI model relationship; when source data lacks a unique column, a Power Query index column can generate one.

A junk dimension consolidates several small, low-cardinality dimensions (such as order status or demographic flags) into one table — typically the Cartesian product of all attribute values plus a surrogate key — to reduce model storage size and Data pane clutter.

A degenerate dimension is a fact-table attribute (such as a sales order number) needed for filtering that is kept directly on the fact table rather than split into its own dimension table, as an accepted exception to the fact/dimension separation rule.

A factless fact table contains only dimension keys and no measures; Microsoft's recommended use of this pattern in Power BI is as a bridging table to implement many-to-many relationships between two dimensions.

Explicit DAX measures are required (rather than relying on implicit column summarization) whenever report authors will query via MDX (including Analyze in Excel or the paginated-report MDX query designer), or when the modeler needs to restrict a column to specific aggregation types.
